sonnet.q1: The fixed popular-items list (fallback), marked `fallback: true`. The model is not called, and the reason (timeout or missing) is counted.
sonnet.q2: The API keeps serving the existing rows already in the online store, and an alert fires after the first failed run. Rows materialized more than 6 hours ago are stale and count as missing, so the API then returns the popular-items fallback instead of old features.
sonnet.q3: No. Shadow output is only logged and never shown to users. Shadow failures cannot affect the user's response: the API does not wait for the queue and drops the message if the queue is full, and workers run on separate capacity.
sonnet.q4: A fixed 10% of users, chosen by hash(user_id) mod 100 < 10, so the same users are always included. This applies only when a `shadow` alias exists. Fallback responses are skipped.
sonnet.q5: It must have spent at least 7 days in shadow, with error rate under 0.5% and p99 inference latency under 80 ms. The ML lead must approve, and the approval is recorded with a name and time. The step 6 feature check must pass again just before the switch. If Product chooses an A/B test, step 12 must also be complete.
sonnet.q6: Not decided. Product has not decided. It is an open optional step 12, and it should not be built until Product decides. The plan works either way.
sonnet.q7: Each instance polls the registry every 15 seconds and reads where the `active` and `previous` aliases point. If one changed, it downloads and loads that version in the background, then atomically swaps to the new active model once fully loaded. No redeploy is needed.
sonnet.q8: A separate shadow worker service takes messages from the queue, loads the `shadow` version and reads that version's features from the online store itself, because the candidate may need features the active model doesn't use. It applies the same freshness rule. Shadow adds no latency because the message is queued only after the API has built its response, and the API never waits for the queue.
sonnet.q9: The queue is bounded. When it is full, the API drops the message without waiting, so shadow samples are lost and the user is unaffected. Dropped messages are counted and alerted on, so a gap in the data is visible. Workers run on their own capacity.
sonnet.q10: Both are recorded in the prediction log, one row per shadowed request. The row holds the request ID, both versions, both item lists, the candidate's inference time and any error. A daily comparison job reads the log and writes a report. It covers days in shadow, error rate, p99 inference latency, sample count and item-list overlap with the active model.
sonnet.q11: Step 6 checks before any alias change to `shadow` or `active`. Every feature the version lists must be defined in the online store, and materialization must have succeeded within the last 6 hours. If the check fails, the alias change is refused with a message naming the missing features. It is re-run just before the switch. Each instance repeats it when loading a model, and if it fails the instance keeps the old active model and alerts.
sonnet.q12: A person decides, or an alert prompts them. They set `active` back to the version in `previous`. Automatic rollback is not planned. It takes effect within a minute because instances already hold `previous` in memory, so no download is needed, and they pick up the alias change at their next 15-second poll. It needs neither the 7-day wait nor ML lead approval, which is an assumption to confirm. It depends on the registry being available.
